Posted July 18, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: I had hoped that Paul Gigot, the new editorial page editor of the Journal, would shake its long-standing addiction to reefer madness.
See

But, alas, it may even have gotten worse. Notice how they use the term " legalizer " as a pejorative.

This is particularly sad in that when The WSJ supports free markets, it uses the classical arguments for personal freedom, warning about the failure of governments to solve problems. But when it comes to cannabis, suddenly everything is different. The government knows best and arresting 750,000 Americans every year isn't even worth mentioning.

In short, they are betraying their own principles and their readers, again.)

From the Wall Street Journal Editorial Page
July 16, 2002

Going To Pot

Tony Blair's new soft-on-marijuana policy has naturally been getting applause from U.S. legalizers. They like the British decision to make possession of marijuana a ticketing offense, in the same category as illegal possession of steroids or anti-depressants.
See

Meanwhile -- though getting much less U.S. media attention -- the Dutch are having second thoughts about their own famously liberal marijuana laws. Last week the Netherlands announced a plan to crack down on the legal " coffee " houses where you can buy cannabis along with your cappuccino.
(MarijuanaNews note: The notion that the Dutch are abandoning the coffee shop system has been a prohibitionist fantasy for some time. When the Christian Democrats got the largest block of seats in the new parliament, much was made of the fact that the new Prime Minister is a prohibitionist.)
See

The arguments for decriminalizing marijuana are well known and not without appeal. And yet the evidence emerging in countries that have legalized (the Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium) supports the view that decriminalization leads to rising drug use and higher crime rates.
(MarijuanaNews note: Really, where is the data to support these claims? First, Belgium has only recently decriminalized possession, so it would be impossible to realistically document any social consequences, good or bad.

Second, the Swiss are going to have a referendum next year on furthering its cannabis policies.

I have not seen any data that supports the notion that crime has increased in Switzerland as a result of its tolerating cannabis.

As for " rising drug use " while the Journal editors were trying " to be fair " they might have noted that the UK has some of the highest rates of all drug use in the EU and a crisis in law enforcement.

In the Netherlands,

And as for moving the shops away from the national borders, there are several problems.

First, The Netherlands is a very small country, and so if the Germans have to drive a few minutes further, what difference is that going to make?

For a map of The Netherlands see

Second, when Belgium decriminalized possession, the government said it was not going to allow coffee shops just yet, so people who wanted to buy cannabis could just cross the open border to get it. That does not sound like a complaint to me.

Finally, there is the fact that the decision on whether a Dutch city will tolerate coffee shops is entirely up to the cities, not the national government. It seems very unlike that a city such as Maastricht, which is in a very narrow strip of Dutch territory between Germany and Belgium is going to close its coffee shops. Obviously, given its location, Maastricht merchants welcome visitors from its very close neighbors. Some of the smaller cities may use it as an excuse to limit the number shops, but that remains to be seen.

In short, this " new policy " is not new and not meaningful.)

Britain has its own bad example in the form of a pilot liberalization in Lambeth, which includes the drugs-ridden south London neighborhood of Brixton. Labour MP Kate Hoey, whose constituency includes Brixton, reports that drug dealers are pushing hard drugs openly on the streets.
(MarijuanaNews note: Yes, she does say that, but that does not make it true. Ms Hoey also claims that cannabis has been " genetically modified " to be more potent.
See

Her constituency seems to favor the experiment.)

Police report an 11% increase in trafficking offenses -- though, to be fair, it wasn't clear whether that was because there are more dealers in the area or more cops.
(MarijuanaNews note: To be fair?? How nice! The stated purpose of the experiment was to free up police resources to go after violent crime and hard drug dealers, so when they arrest more hard drug dealers, this is cited as evidence that the policy was a failure. Now if arrests of hard drug dealers had gone down, what would that have proved? That the policy was a failure? And if arrests were unchanged? That too would be proof of failure!

In their effort " to be fair " the editors overlooked the fact that violent crime in the area has gone down sharply.)
See

For the U.S., the lesson would appear to be to beware legalizers bearing British gifts. Mr. Blair's proposal may sail through the House of Commons, but we're willing to wager that like the Dutch the British will regret the decision once they notice the rise in drug use.
(MarijuanaNews note: I'll take that bet! In fact, most of Europe is moving toward the Dutch model. It is especially shameful that the Journal does not mention the cannabis arrest data for either country.)

The U.S. is better off just saying no.

Copyright: 2002 Dow Jones & Company, Inc.
(MarijuanaNews note: Meanwhile in France, there has been a unfortunate consequence of the reelection of the corrupt President Jacque Chirac. The WSJ should like this.

Frightened by a threat from the far right, he has appointed Nicolas Sarkozy, a hard line prohibitionist, as Interior Minister. The Guardian recently reported that Sarkozy has said that " The words 'soft' and 'drugs' will always be incompatible. There is quite simply no such thing as a 'soft drug'. We are determined to fight against drug dealers and against drugs of whatever kind wherever, whenever and however we can. "
See

That is very unfortunate and reverses some progress over the last few years.
